"In this work we systematically examine whether dynamics prediction is essential for physical reasoning by contrasting two learning paradigms: Learning from Dynamics (LfD), which relies on predicted future states, and Learning from Intuition (LfI), which bases decisions solely on static scene analysis. We first demonstrate that a simple LfI classifier attains performance comparable to or better than state-of-the-art LfD methods on the PHYRE benchmark. Next, using ground-truth dynamics as an oracle, we establish an upper bound showing that perfect future information can markedly boost reasoning accuracy, confirming the theoretical value of dynamics. We then replace the oracle with predicted dynamics from a strong forward-prediction model and observe that approximation errors rapidly degrade performance, causing LfD to collapse toward the LfI regime. Finally, extensive experiments across multiple LfI architectures reveal that intuition-based approaches are not only simpler but also more robust in practice. Collectively, these findings clarify the role of dynamics prediction in physical reasoning, delineate its practical limitations, and highlight promising directions for improving future-prediction modules."
